data.title: Belušské Slatiny – Hradište, a Púchov culture refuge above Mojtínske vráta
data.excerpt: A craggy massif above Prvé mojtínske vráta carries a kidney-shaped hillfort of about 60 × 25 m, with the ruins of a stony-earthen rampart of box construction that in places reached a height of 3–4 metres. The sparse finds, the burnt clay and the fire-cracked stones identify it almost with certainty as a refuge of the Púchov culture, which fell victim to Germanic tribes in the first decade AD.
data.metaTitle: Belušské Slatiny – Hradište above Mojtínske vráta

children.text: The site of Hradište (the older name Ostré vŕšky) lies on the right bank of the Slatinský (Podhradský) stream above Prvé mojtínske vráta (the First Mojtín Gates), about 1.5 km from Belušské Slatiny in the direction of Mojtín. The craggy massif projects steeply across the direction of the valley (a west–east orientation). It forms the end of a narrow ridge about three hundred metres long, the opposite end of which has a similar shape (an extensive hilltop settlement of the Púchov culture was identified there later – see the documentation).
THE HILLFORT ITSELF (appendix no. 1 – sketch of the site)

blocks.caption: A view of the hillfort, by Vladimír Ruček
blocks.alt: A view of the hillfort, by Vladimír Ruček

children.text: On the top of the massif there are distinct remains of a hillfort of kidney shape, measuring approximately 60 × 25 m. From the highest point in the western part (spot height 518.8 m) the terrain slopes gently away from the ridge into the southern slope. At the edge, by the defences, there is an artificially created terrace 2–3 m wide. Beneath it lie the massive ruins of the original defences. According to the remains, they consisted of a stony-earthen rampart of box construction, filled with limestone blocks 20–60 cm in diameter and with earth. On the evidence of a few worked stones, there may have been a stone facing on the outer side of the rampart. In places the rampart must have reached a height of 3–4 metres and a width of about 1.5 m at the crest (judging from the terrain and the volume of stone in the ruins). The wooden palisade on the crest of the rampart continued around the perimeter of the hillfort, where on the northern side it formed the only defence above the steep slope of the hill. The distribution of the ruins and the configuration of the terrain suggest that the entrance into the hillfort was from the southern side, by the path from the main ridge of the massif. Above the entrance there probably stood a wooden gateway. At the eastern edge of the hillfort a smaller watchtower may be assumed.
FINDS AND THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THEIR DISCOVERY

Beneath the ruins of the rampart on the western slope of the ridge a small hoard of iron objects (12 pieces) was found around the circumference of a tree whose roots had pushed the objects to the surface. Together with them lay two sherds of handmade thick-walled pottery containing siliceous sand, fired to a brown colour (1). Inside the hillfort further sherds of a greyish-black colour containing siliceous sand and a piece of daub were found on the surface (2). Beneath the ruins of the rampart, on the outer side, numerous stones cracked by intense heat were found, one of them with the remains of the timber construction of the rampart (3). In the stone ruins near the presumed gateway a fragment of a stone quern for grinding grain was found, with a circular hole 4 cm in diameter (4). Inside the defences there is a thin black occupation layer. On the southern slope below the rampart, over a width of 2–3 m, clay burnt to a red colour predominates as a remnant of a massive fire (5).

children.text: OTHER INSIGHTS ABOUT THE SITE AND ITS SURROUNDINGS

According to the informant Dr S. Mika, no tales or legends about this site are so far known in the surroundings of Beluša and Mojtín (apart from the fact that the ruins of an old fortification are to be found there). On a military map from the beginning of the 1950s and also on a tourist map of 1985 the site is marked as Ostré vŕšky. Newer maps give it as Hradište. In the available historical, archaeological and tourist sources, however, there is no mention of the site.

The site of Hradište was undoubtedly known long ago to the inhabitants of the surrounding settlements, and they probably also carried off a quantity of surface finds. Apart from one smaller hollow, there are no visible traces of digging.

On the evidence of the finds, so far not numerous (pottery sherds, iron objects), the character of the defences and the burnt clay and stones in their vicinity, the hillfort can be identified almost with certainty as a refuge of the people of the Púchov culture (the end of the La Tène period and the beginning of the Roman period). Together with dozens of other hillforts and small forts in north-western Slovakia it fell victim to Germanic tribes in the first decade AD, in the period of the so-called catastrophic horizon. The hillfort served the inhabitants of one or more settlements in the Mojtín valley, which were probably situated at the northern foot of the hill (the present-day cottage settlement) or in Belušské Slatiny. So far, however, no traces of occupation from this period have been found there. The absence of finds at Hradište itself does not yet allow it to be dated to any other periods.
During more detailed investigation of the site and its surroundings, an extensive hilltop settlement of the Púchov culture was identified on the opposite side of the ridge (above the quarry).
